prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a rare case where a sharp, quantitative theoretical prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, 2011, with a specific magic angle and flat bands) was followed seven years later by an experimental discovery (correlated insulators and superconductivity, 2018) that opened an entirely new platform, moire quantum materials, now reproduced in many groups and many stacking geometries. It fits the discovery criterion well: the central observations are concrete and reproducible, and the field it created is broad. The theory-plus-experiment pairing is clean and the three credited names map onto it. Seeing the whole ballot set, this candidate carries the strongest first-place support (two) together with top-three placements from four members, and I do not think that support is merely a matter of fashion; the underlying physics is original in the way a prediction followed by a surprising confirmation is original.
statement.case_against: The field is young and the mechanism of the superconductivity, and the exact nature of several correlated phases, are still contested, so the interpretation that a prize citation would rest on is partly open. Experimental credit is also concentrated: the 2018 papers had first authors and collaborators (notably Yuan Cao and Valla Fatemi, and parallel work by Dean and colleagues on moire heterostructures) who cannot be named under the three-person limit, and a prize would leave real credit unrecognised. By comparison, topological insulators (B012) are twice as old, more thoroughly confirmed, and were ranked in the top four by seven of eight members, so a fair objection is that B047 is being preferred to a more mature and more broadly supported candidate.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B047 fifth, calling it strong and original but fast-moving and probably early for a prize, and proposed only two names (MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero) to keep the theory-experiment pairing clean.
responses.response: I take the timing worry seriously, but I think it is weaker here than for most young fields. The prize criterion is the discovery, and what is established is the flat-band prediction and the observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states, which have been reproduced across many labs and platforms. The unsettled pairing mechanism is a question about what the discovery means, not whether it is real; compare how long mechanism questions about high-Tc superconductors have remained open without making the discovery itself premature. On the names I disagree with a two-person prize: Bistritzer is the first author on the 2011 prediction, and the magic angle is a specific quantitative result of that calculation. Dropping him would credit the idea to MacDonald alone, which misdescribes who did the work, and the three-person limit gives room for him.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked active-matter hydrodynamics first and B047 second, endorsing the theory-plus-experiment pairing but suggesting Jarillo-Herrero and MacDonald with Bistritzer's role as co-author of the key calculation noted.
responses.response: I agree on the structure and mostly on the names, and I want to hold the line on including Bistritzer rather than treating him as a footnote. I would add a qualification to your own first choice: active matter is intellectually deep, but I find the experimental confirmation of its sharpest predictions (long-range polar order in two dimensions, giant number fluctuations) less decisive and less tied to one identifiable discovery, and the credit is spread across Vicsek, Toner, Tu, Ramaswamy and others. I would not rank it above B047 or B012 as a prize case today, though I accept it is a serious candidate for the longer term and I understand why a statistical physicist would put it first.

responses.point: Kroll ranked optical lattice clocks first with Katori and Ye as the natural pair, and placed twisted bilayer graphene seventh, outside his specialty and with the interpretation of superconductivity unsettled.
responses.response: The clock case is clean in attribution, and I rank it fourth rather than low; Katori and Ye are an unusually unambiguous pair and the maturity is real, with several labs at the 1e-18 level. My difference is about breadth of the discovery: a lattice clock is an extraordinary improvement in a measurement, whereas moire materials changed what questions a whole community can ask about correlated matter. I also note the redefinition of the second is still pending, so part of the clock's practical impact is prospective. I would keep B019 as my second alternative to B012 and would find it a respectable outcome if the committee prefers it.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked lattice clocks first and topological insulators second, with B047 not among her eight; she regarded QSH as conceptually deep and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree that B012 is deeply established and I share the view that it is arguably overdue; that is why I list it as my first alternative and ranked it second. Where I differ is that the Kane-Mele and HgTe trio leaves the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction and the three-dimensional topological insulator work (Fu, Kane, Mele; Hsieh, Hasan) outside the credited names, and Zhang is deceased, so the attribution is the more fragmented of the two. The 2016 prize on topological phase transitions also covers part of the conceptual ground. B047 has a tidier prediction-then-discovery chain, which is why I put it ahead.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the unresolved superconducting mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene as a maturity problem or only an open follow-up question.
Whether the credited three-person set can fairly omit the first authors of the 2018 experiments and other moire pioneers, and whether Bistritzer should be included alongside MacDonald.
How much the 2016 prize on topological phases should discount B012 relative to B047, since that could change my ordering of the two.
Whether B012 or B047 better serves the committee given that B012 has far broader opening support (seven of eight members) than B047 (six of eight).
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My connections (Gross, Rubinstein, Van Riet, Uppsala theory group) are in high-energy theory and cosmology and do not touch any shortlisted candidate or credited name. I note only that as a theorist I may be inclined to favour candidates built on a decisive prediction, and I have tried to weigh the experimental maturity case for B012 and B019 accordingly.
